workedExamples.title: Joint vs. marginal relative frequency in a 2×2 table

steps.prompt: A survey of 100 students records two yes/no questions: "Do you play a sport?" and "Do you like math?" The counts are: play & like = 30, play & dislike = 20, don't play & like = 25, don't play & dislike = 25. First, organize these into a 2×2 table and find the row totals, column totals, and grand total.
steps.reveal: Rows = play / don't play, columns = like / dislike. Play row: 30 + 20 = 50. Don't-play row: 25 + 25 = 50. Like column: 30 + 25 = 55. Dislike column: 20 + 25 = 45. Grand total: 50 + 50 = 100 (and 55 + 45 = 100, which checks). Every total must trace back to the four cells, so an auditor can rebuild the table from the cells alone.

steps.prompt: A JOINT relative frequency answers "what fraction of EVERYONE falls in this single cell?" Find the joint relative frequency of students who play a sport AND like math, as a percent.
steps.reveal: Joint = cell ÷ grand total = 30 ÷ 100 = 0.30 = 30%. The denominator for a joint relative frequency is always the GRAND total, because we are comparing one cell against the whole group.

steps.prompt: A MARGINAL relative frequency answers "what fraction of everyone falls in this whole row or whole column?" Find the marginal relative frequency of students who play a sport, as a percent.
steps.reveal: Marginal = row total ÷ grand total = 50 ÷ 100 = 0.50 = 50%. The numerator is the ROW total (a margin of the table), not a single cell.

steps.prompt: Why is the joint answer (30%) different from the marginal answer (50%), even though both involve students who play a sport?
steps.reveal: Joint counts only the cell — play AND like math (30 people). Marginal counts the entire play row — like OR dislike math (50 people). Confusing the two is the joint-vs-marginal trap: the joint cell is always a piece of the larger marginal total, so reporting 50% when the question asked for the single cell over-counts by including the 20 who dislike math.

workedExamples.title: Row percent vs. column percent: choosing the denominator

steps.prompt: Use the same table: play & like = 30, play & dislike = 20, don't play & like = 25, don't play & dislike = 25 (grand total 100; play row total = 50; like column total = 55). A conditional (row or column) percent uses a denominator that is NOT the grand total. First write the two totals you might divide the cell 30 by.
steps.reveal: The cell 30 sits in the play ROW (total 50) and the like COLUMN (total 55). So the two candidate denominators are 50 (its row total) and 55 (its column total). Picking the right one is the whole game.

steps.prompt: Question A: "Of the students who PLAY a sport, what percent like math?" Which total is the denominator, and what is the percent?
steps.reveal: "Of the students who play" fixes the group to the play ROW, so divide by the row total 50: 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60 = 60%. The phrase "of the [row group]" tells you the row total is the denominator.

steps.prompt: Question B: "Of the students who LIKE math, what percent play a sport?" Which total is the denominator, and what is the percent?
steps.reveal: "Of the students who like math" fixes the group to the like COLUMN, so divide by the column total 55: 30 ÷ 55 ≈ 0.545 = 54.5%. Same cell (30), different denominator, different meaning.

steps.prompt: Both questions involve the same cell (30). Why are 60% and 54.5% both correct but to DIFFERENT questions?
steps.reveal: The denominator must match the group named after the word "of." "Of those who play" → divide by the row total (50). "Of those who like math" → divide by the column total (55). Using 55 when the question said "of those who play" is the row-column-percent-confusion trap: right cell, wrong denominator, wrong answer.

p1.prompt: A coach charts 100 at-bats in a 2×2 table by count and outcome. Ahead in the count & hit = 30, ahead & out = 20, behind & hit = 10, behind & out = 40. What fraction of ALL 100 at-bats were ahead in the count AND a hit? Answer as a percent.
hints: A joint relative frequency divides one cell by the grand total of 100.

p1.prompt: From the same chart of 100 at-bats: ahead & hit = 30, ahead & out = 20, behind & hit = 10, behind & out = 40. What percent of ALL at-bats were ahead in the count (the whole 'ahead' row)? Answer as a percent.
hints: A marginal relative frequency divides a row total by the grand total.
Ahead row total = 30 + 20 = 50; then 50 ÷ 100.

p1.prompt: Same 100 at-bats: ahead & hit = 30, ahead & out = 20, behind & hit = 10, behind & out = 40. Of the at-bats that were AHEAD in the count, what percent were hits? Answer as a percent.
hints: 'Of the at-bats that were ahead' means divide by the ahead ROW total (50), not a column total.

p1.prompt: Same 100 at-bats: ahead & hit = 30, ahead & out = 20, behind & hit = 10, behind & out = 40. Of the at-bats that ended in a HIT, what percent came when the batter was ahead in the count? Answer as a percent.
hints: 'Of the at-bats that ended in a hit' means divide by the HIT column total.
Hit column total = 30 + 10 = 40; then 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75.

p1.prompt: Same 200 plate appearances: starters & on-base = 80, starters & out = 60, bench & on-base = 20, bench & out = 40. Of the STARTERS' plate appearances, what percent ended on base? Answer as a percent (to the nearest percent).
hints: 'Of the starters' means divide by the starters ROW total (140), not the on-base column.
80 ÷ 140 ≈ 0.5714, which rounds to 57%.

p1.prompt: Same 200 plate appearances: starters & on-base = 80, starters & out = 60, bench & on-base = 20, bench & out = 40. Of the plate appearances that ended ON BASE, what percent were by starters? Answer as a percent.
hints: 'Of the appearances that ended on base' means divide by the ON-BASE column total.
On-base column total = 80 + 20 = 100; then 80 ÷ 100 = 0.80.

p2.prompt: A two-way table charts 200 at-bats. Cells: vs lefty & hit = 36, vs lefty & out = 84, vs righty & hit = 32, vs righty & out = 48. Is the value '36 hits vs lefties out of 200 at-bats' a JOINT relative frequency or a MARGINAL relative frequency?
hints: A single cell over the grand total is a JOINT relative frequency; a row or column total over the grand total is MARGINAL.
36 is one cell, not a whole row or column.

p2.prompt: Same 200 at-bats: vs lefty & hit = 36, vs lefty & out = 84, vs righty & hit = 32, vs righty & out = 48. What is the MARGINAL relative frequency of at-bats versus lefty pitchers? Answer as a percent.
hints: Marginal means a whole row total over the grand total.
vs-lefty row total = 36 + 84 = 120; then 120 ÷ 200.

p2.prompt: Same 200 at-bats: vs lefty & hit = 36, vs lefty & out = 84, vs righty & hit = 32, vs righty & out = 48. To find the percent of AT-BATS VERSUS LEFTIES that were hits, which total do you divide 36 by?
hints: 'Of the at-bats versus lefties' fixes the group to that ROW, so use the row total.
Divide by 120, not by the hit column.

p2.prompt: Same 200 at-bats: vs lefty & hit = 36, vs lefty & out = 84, vs righty & hit = 32, vs righty & out = 48. Of the at-bats that ended in a HIT, what percent came against righties? Answer as a percent (to the nearest percent).
hints: 'Of the at-bats that ended in a hit' means divide by the HIT column total.
Hit column total = 36 + 32 = 68; then 32 ÷ 68 ≈ 0.470, which rounds to 47%.

p2.prompt: Same 100 swings: contact & in play = 45, contact & whiff = 5, power & in play = 20, power & whiff = 30. To find the percent of CONTACT SWINGS that stayed in play, which total do you divide 45 by?
hints: 'Of the contact swings' fixes the group to that ROW, so use the row total.

p2.prompt: Same 100 swings: contact & in play = 45, contact & whiff = 5, power & in play = 20, power & whiff = 30. Of the swings that stayed IN PLAY, what percent were power swings? Answer as a percent (to the nearest percent).
hints: 'Of the swings that stayed in play' means divide by the IN-PLAY column total.
In-play column total = 45 + 20 = 65; then 20 ÷ 65 ≈ 0.308, which rounds to 31%.
